design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analyses of logit-transformed proportions (PROSPERO CRD42020179683) of the prevalence of cocaine-induced psychosis (CIP) in people who use cocaine and have no primary psychotic disorder or mood disorder with psychotic features. CIP combines cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms (CIPS: symptom questionnaires such as the Cocaine Experience Questionnaire and the SAPS-CIP, or study-specific questions, in two studies a single symptom) with cocaine-induced psychotic disorder diagnosed on DSM criteria (CIPD/SIPD: PRISM or MINI interviews). Two pooled groups: current CIP in current use (3 studies, n=102, two of them laboratory cocaine-administration studies) and lifetime CIP in lifetime use (17 studies, n=5286, almost all treatment samples). In all, 20 studies and 5388 participants; subgroup analyses by definition, risk of bias, instrument, region, sample size and share with dependence; meta-regression on year of publication.
can_establish: How often people in cocaine treatment samples (and in two small laboratory samples) reported, or were diagnosed with, cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms or disorder in studies published up to 2020, and how strongly the figure depends on the definition: about 68% lifetime for symptoms against about 16% for a DSM disorder.
cannot_establish: The prevalence in people who use cocaine outside treatment (no general-population sample); that cocaine alone produced the symptoms (other drug use was common and could not be analysed); effects of dose or route (not analysable); or a single meaningful prevalence across definitions (I² 97%, and the overall interval printed is narrower than a standard random-effects interval, editors' calculation). Every figure is provisional until the published corrigendum is read.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES to 31 August 2020, limited to English-language studies of adult humans, with reference-list snowballing (p. 2); the flow chart also lists ClinicalTrials.gov (70 records) and the EU clinical trials register (45) (p. 3). Participants in the included studies were people seeking or receiving treatment (mostly outpatient addiction services; one inpatient service; one psychiatric emergency unit), plus volunteers in three laboratory cocaine-challenge studies (p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: cross-sectional, case-control or cohort studies of people with current or past cocaine use (use, abuse, dependence) that excluded people with primary psychotic disorders or mood disorders with psychotic features, or reported them separately, and that reported the prevalence of CIP (p. 2). Excluded: CIP diagnosed only by retrospective chart review; samples limited to people with CIP; samples whose main drug was not cocaine; no prevalence of CIPS, CIPD or SIPD reported; case reports and qualitative studies (p. 2). Three laboratory challenge studies were included although the listed designs do not cover them (p. 3).
sample.demographics: Mean sample size printed as 269.2 (23 to 2192); mean share of men 68% (49–100%), two studies men only; mean age 37.0 years (study means 23–45); mean age at first cocaine use 22.2 (11 studies, n=1888); mean years of cocaine use printed as 22.4 (7 studies, n=916). USA 13 studies, Spain 4, French Caribbean 1, Canada 1, Brazil 1 (p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: Clinical samples throughout: the authors state the estimates could be inflated by selection and admission-rate (Berkson) bias (p. 7). English only and no grey literature. The current-use estimate rests on two laboratory self-administration studies of paranoia (12 of 28; 29 of 44) and one psychiatric emergency series (12 of 30) (Fig. 2, p. 4). The largest lifetime study (Zaytas 2013, 2192 participants, 41% of the lifetime total) and Floyd 2006 have no entry in the reference list, and Cubells 2005 and Tang 2007, whose reference entries share authors, are entered with identical counts (181 of 243) (Fig. 3, p. 5; pp. 7–8).

exposure.measurement: Each included study assessed cocaine dependence with DSM-III or DSM-IV (p. 3); otherwise exposure is whatever each study reported (history of use, dependence).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable: dose and severity of dependence were reported too rarely, and route could not be analysed (pp. 5–7). Two lifetime studies reported a higher estimated lifetime cocaine dose in people with CIP, and one laboratory study reported that CIP was dose-dependent (pp. 6–7).
exposure.polysubstance: Reported in few studies: current use of alcohol 39.5% (2 studies), opioids 50.1% (2), cannabis 39.7% (3), other stimulants 30.8% (1); lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% (3), opioids 30% (2), cannabis 32% (2) (p. 3). Its contribution to CIP could not be determined (p. 6); the authors argue that cannabis-induced psychosis is an unlikely explanation of the findings (p. 6) and that cocaine cannot be shown to be directly responsible (p. 6).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; lifetime CIP was assessed retrospectively in most studies (p. 6).

comparison.controls: None (prevalence among people who use cocaine).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of psychosis and other vulnerability factors were not analysable; individual-level data were not available (p. 6).

outcomes.instruments: CIPS: Cocaine Experience Questionnaire (6 lifetime studies), SAPS-CIP (1), study-specific questions (6), and paranoia during laboratory cocaine administration (2 current-use studies); CIPD: PRISM semi-structured interview (4 studies, 3 lifetime and 1 current) and MINI (1) (pp. 4–5). Risk of bias of included studies: the Hoy et al. (2012) tool for prevalence studies, 10 items plus a summary judgment, applied independently by two authors; items without enough information were rated high risk, and studies defining CIPS by a single symptom were rated high risk on case definition (p. 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The PRISM was designed to separate substance-induced from primary disorders (p. 4); the CEQ and SAPS-CIP quantify symptoms ranging from transient to persistent (p. 6).
outcomes.operationalization: CIP = current CIP in people currently using cocaine, or lifetime CIP in people with lifetime use; CIPS and CIPD were combined after the authors found that most studies measured symptoms rather than disorder (p. 2). For three PRISM studies the prevalence had to be extracted after removing patients with primary psychosis (p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The 24 are the pooled estimates reported in the text: 2 main pools, 21 subgroup and sensitivity estimates, and 1 meta-regression; subgroup differences were judged by residual heterogeneity, not by formal tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; screening and extraction were done in duplicate (p. 2).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects meta-analysis of logit proportions. Current use (3 studies, n=102): 50.2% (95% CI 32.0–68.4), I²=66%; without the Mooney laboratory study 41.4% (29.5–54.4), I²=0%; CIPD 40.0% (14.9–71.7), one study; CIPS 55.2% (32.8–75.7), two laboratory studies, I²=72% (p. 4; Fig. 2). Lifetime use (17 studies, n=5286): 55.6% (50.2–61.0), I²=97%, τ²=0.1597 printed in Fig. 3; CIPS 68.4% (62.8–73.5), 13 studies; CIPD 16% (10.6–23.2), 4 studies; I²=89% in each (pp. 4–5; Fig. 3). Low risk of bias only (14 lifetime studies): 55.6% (50.5–60.6), I²=97%; CIPS 68.3% (63.2–73.1); CIPD 11.7% (7.6–17.4), I²=0% (pp. 4–5). By instrument: CEQ 70.1% (62.6–76.7), 6 studies; SAPS-CIP 84.2% (69.0–92.7), 1 study; study-specific questions 63.4% (55.2–70.9), 6 studies; PRISM 11.7% (7.4–17.9), 3 studies; MINI 35.8% (18.9–57.1), 1 study (p. 5). By region: North America 66.5% (57.6–74.3); South America and the Caribbean 56.1% (34.2–75.5); Europe 25.1% (15.1–38.6). By study size: under 60 participants 69.2% (52.8–81.9); 60–200, 36.2% (22.8–52.3); over 200, 59.8% (46.7–71.7). By dependence: majority dependent (4 studies) 53.5% (33.4–72.5); all dependent (13) 54.3% (44.8–67.2) (p. 5). Year of publication did not explain heterogeneity (p. 6). Editors' calculations from the study counts printed in Figs 2 and 3: the printed lifetime overall estimate, interval and study weights are reproduced exactly only when the between-study variance estimated within the CIPS and CIPD subgroups (τ²=0.1597) is used for the overall model; a standard DerSimonian–Laird random-effects model of all 17 studies gives the same 55.6% with τ²=0.593, a 95% CI of 46.0–64.8% and a 95% prediction interval of 18.7–87.2%. CIPS with its own τ² (0.138): 68.4% (63.1–73.2), prediction interval 47.8–83.6%; CIPD with its own τ² (0.482): 16.0% (8.5–28.3). Without Tang 2007 (identical counts to Cubells 2005): overall 54.2% (44.1–64.0), CIPS 67.7% (62.1–72.9).
analysis.covariates: None at review level; individual-level variables could not be examined (p. 6).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42020179683, registered on 14 July 2020 (p. 2), 24 days before the manuscript was received on 7 August 2020 (p. 1); the search is dated to 31 August 2020, after submission (presumably updated in revision, which is not stated). The planned focus on CIPD was changed to CIP, combining CIPS and CIPD, after the search showed that most studies measured symptoms (p. 2). The registry record was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Meta-regressions were planned for several moderators, but only year of publication was explored, because individual-level data were unavailable (pp. 3, 6). Per-study characteristics and risk-of-bias judgments are only in supplements (Tables S1–S2) that were not read.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The current-use group has 3 studies and 102 people, and several subgroups rest on one study; all subgroup analyses are study-level comparisons among few studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In studies of people in cocaine treatment, about two thirds reported having had cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms at some time (68.4%, 13 studies, I² 89%), while about one in six met DSM criteria for a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (16%, 4 studies); the two cannot be summarized by one figure (I² 97%). The current-use estimate (50.2%) comes from 102 people in two laboratory self-administration studies and one psychiatric emergency series.
interpretation_gap.claimed: This PDF has no abstract. The Discussion reports one overall prevalence per group (50.2% and 55.6%) as high and calls the definition of CIP the only moderator accounting for heterogeneity (p. 6), although the definition subgroups left residual I² of 72% and 89% (pp. 4–5) and the overall lifetime interval is narrower than a standard random-effects interval (editors' calculation). The title speaks of people who use cocaine in general; the Conclusions more accurately restrict the finding to people in contact with health services (p. 7). The Discussion states that cocaine cannot be shown to be directly responsible, because other drugs were used in all studies, and that cross-sectional retrospective designs preclude causal conclusions (p. 6), yet the outcome is called cocaine-induced throughout. The clinical-relevance section extrapolates a risk of transition to schizophrenia from amphetamine data (p. 7) and recommends systematic screening, which these data do not test.

timeline.event: Lecomte et al.: meta-analysis giving a lifetime prevalence of substance-induced psychotic disorder of 42.7% in people with methamphetamine use disorders (as cited, p. 6)

Meta-analysis of transition from substance-induced psychoses to schizophrenia: no study of transition after cocaine-induced psychotic disorder; 22% after amphetamine-induced psychotic disorder (as cited, p. 1)
This review, described by its authors as the first meta-analysis of the prevalence of CIP (p. 6)
Corrigendum published (10.1016/j.pnpbp.2021.110434); not read for this card, because the file saved under its name is a different document

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of the prevalence of cocaine-induced psychosis identified by its authors. Its definition-specific estimates (symptoms about 68%, DSM disorder about 16%, lifetime, in treatment samples) are the usable results; the single pooled figures and the current-use figure are not. Until the corrigendum is read, every number on this card is provisional.

funding.declared_conflicts: Stefan Kaiser has received royalties for cognitive test and training software from Schuhfried; Michel Sabe and Nan Zhao declare no conflict of interest (p. 7).
funding.affiliations_note: Division of Adult Psychiatry, Department of Psychiatry, Geneva University Hospitals (p. 1). Open access under a CC BY licence (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A general-population cohort of people who use cocaine, assessed with structured interviews that separate transient symptoms from DSM substance-induced psychotic disorder and from primary psychosis, with dose, route and other drug use measured prospectively, would give the prevalence outside treatment and how it depends on use; an individual-participant meta-analysis of existing treatment cohorts with a common definition is the achievable near-term step.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with current or lifetime cocaine use without primary psychosis), condition (CIP, as CIPS and CIPD), designs and settings specified; prevalence needs no comparator.

PROSPERO CRD42020179683, registered 14 July 2020, 24 days before submission, so it cannot be confirmed that methods were fixed before the work began; the change from CIPD to combined CIP is stated and justified (p. 2).
Designs are listed without an explanation, and three laboratory challenge studies outside the listed designs were included.

Five databases, search terms and snowballing, with two trial registries in the flow chart; but English-only and adult-only limits without justification and no grey literature (item 4 read as written, decision p-amstar2-item4).
Titles, abstracts and methods inspected independently by two authors (p. 2).
Two authors with a predefined form; disagreements resolved by consensus or a third reviewer (p. 2).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons and counts in the flow chart and three named exclusions (p. 3), but no list of the 206 excluded full texts; the supplements were not read, and none is described as such a list.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: study-level details are only in Supplementary Table S1, which was not read; the article gives pooled characteristics and the counts in the forest plots.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A tool designed for prevalence studies (Hoy et al., 2012), covering selection and measurement, applied independently by two authors (p. 2); per-study ratings are in an unread supplement, and the summary counts in the text are inconsistent (reporting issues).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects pooling of logit proportions suits prevalence data, but the headline pools combine laboratory paranoia with clinical diagnoses and single-symptom with DSM definitions (I² 97%); the overall lifetime interval is reproduced only with the within-subgroup τ², which narrows it (editors' calculation); and two reports with identical counts from overlapping author groups are pooled as separate studies.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Re-analysis restricted to low-risk studies (14 lifetime studies) reported (pp. 4–5).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Selection and admission-rate bias, the cross-sectional retrospective designs and the low-risk-only analysis are discussed (pp. 6–7).
Subgroup analyses by definition, instrument, region, size and dependence, a meta-regression on year, and discussion of the residual heterogeneity (pp. 4–7).
Not investigated, on the argument that publication does not depend on the prevalence a study reports (p. 2); a subgroup by study size is the only related analysis.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Internal funding and one author's royalties declared (p. 7).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from Supplementary Table S1, which was not read; the overall rating does not depend on it. Four critical items are not met (4, 7, 11 and 15) and one is met only in part (2), which gives critically low confidence. That rating does not make the review useless: it reports its estimates by definition and by instrument, and its forest plots print every study's counts, so the definition-specific estimates can be used and checked. The card may be cited for the lifetime prevalence of cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms (about 68%) and of DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (about 16%) among people in cocaine treatment, with the provisos that these are treatment samples, that other drug use was common, and that the corrigendum has not been read; the single pooled figures (50.2% and 55.6%) should not be cited as a prevalence among people who use cocaine, and the current-use figure not at all.

key_findings.finding: 20 studies (5388 participants) were included from 1688 unique records and 226 full texts: 3 studies of current CIP in current use (102 participants) and 17 of lifetime CIP in lifetime use (5286); all cross-sectional except three laboratory cocaine-challenge studies.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Search results; 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1 (p. 3); 3.5 and 3.6, 1st paragraphs (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Participants were people seeking or receiving treatment (mostly outpatient addiction services; one inpatient service); the current-use group consisted of one psychiatric emergency series and two laboratory self-administration studies. Mean 68% men; mean age 37.0; USA 13 studies, Spain 4, French Caribbean, Canada and Brazil 1 each.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Studies and patient characteristics, 1st, 5th and 6th paragraphs (6th begins p. 3, ends p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Lifetime CIP in lifetime use: 55.6% (95% CI 50.2–61.0), 17 studies, I²=97%. By definition: psychotic symptoms (CIPS) 68.4% (62.8–73.5), 13 studies; DSM psychotic disorder (CIPD) 16% (10.6–23.2), 4 studies; I²=89% in each.
key_findings.locator: 3.6 CIP in lifetime cocaine users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 4); Fig. 3 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts in Fig. 3: the printed overall interval uses the within-subgroup τ² (0.1597); a standard random-effects model of all 17 studies gives 55.6% (46.0–64.8), τ²=0.593, prediction interval 18.7–87.2%. With its own τ² the CIPD estimate is 16.0% (8.5–28.3). Provisional until the corrigendum is read.

key_findings.finding: Current CIP in current use: 50.2% (32.0–68.4), 3 studies, n=102, I²=66%. The studies: paranoia during laboratory cocaine administration in 12 of 28 (Kalayasiri 2006b) and 29 of 44 (Mooney 2006), and CIPD in 12 of 30 at a psychiatric emergency unit (Elangovan 1993); without Mooney 2006, 41.4% (29.5–54.4).
key_findings.locator: 3.5 CIP in current cocaine users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 2

key_findings.finding: By instrument (lifetime): CEQ 70.1% (62.6–76.7), 6 studies, I²=50; SAPS-CIP 84.2% (69.0–92.7), 1 study; study-specific questions 63.4% (55.2–70.9), 6 studies, I²=94%; PRISM 11.7% (7.4–17.9), 3 studies; MINI 35.8% (18.9–57.1), 1 study.
Restricting to studies at low risk of bias (14 lifetime studies) left the estimates almost unchanged: 55.6% (50.5–60.6); CIPS 68.3% (63.2–73.1); CIPD 11.7% (7.6–17.4), I²=0%.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: these values are reproduced when three lifetime studies are dropped (best fit: Vergara-Moragues 2014, Miguel 2018, Willi 2017), consistent with 14 low-risk studies, not the 15 stated in 3.4.

key_findings.finding: By region: North America 66.5% (57.6–74.3), South America and the Caribbean 56.1% (34.2–75.5), Europe 25.1% (15.1–38.6); by study size: under 60 participants 69.2%, 60–200 participants 36.2%, over 200 participants 59.8%; by share with dependence: 53.5% and 54.3%. None reduced the residual heterogeneity (I² 95–97%).

Other drug use was reported in few studies: current alcohol 39.5% (2 studies), opioids 50.1% (2), cannabis 39.7% (3), other stimulants 30.8% (1); lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% (3), opioids 30% (2), cannabis 32% (2). Its contribution could not be analysed, and neither could dose, severity of dependence or route.

The authors state that the estimates could be inflated by selection and admission-rate (Berkson) bias in treatment samples, and that cross-sectional designs with retrospective assessment do not allow conclusions about cause.
Publication bias was not investigated; the authors argue that whether a study reporting a prevalence is published does not depend on the prevalence it reports.

reporting_issues.issue: This PDF has no abstract or keywords: the article opens with the Introduction (p. 1). A corrigendum was published (10.1016/j.pnpbp.2021.110434), but it was not available: the file saved under its name is a different document.
reporting_issues.consequence: What the corrigendum changed cannot be settled from this card: it may concern the missing abstract, any of the figures in these issues, or something else. Treat every number as provisional until it is read.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 3 prints the same τ² (0.1597) for the lifetime overall model, 55.6% (50.2–61.0), as for each subgroup, and the shared τ² widens single-study subgroup intervals: Elangovan 1993 (12 of 30) has its own interval of 24–58% but a printed subgroup interval of 14.9–71.7% (Fig. 2). Editors' calculation from the Fig. 3 counts: the printed overall estimate, interval and weights are reproduced exactly only when the between-study variance estimated within the CIPS and CIPD subgroups is applied to the overall model; a standard random-effects model of the 17 studies gives the same point estimate with a 95% CI of 46.0–64.8% (τ²=0.593).
reporting_issues.consequence: The overall lifetime interval overstates precision by about half; the definition-specific estimates are the citable ones.

reporting_issues.issue: Cubells 2005 and Tang 2007 are entered with identical counts (181 of 243 each), and their reference entries share authors (Cubells, Tang, Farrer); the review discusses sample overlap only for Araos 2015 and Pavon 2013 (p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: If the two reports share a sample, 243 people are counted twice; without Tang 2007 the CIPS estimate is 67.7% (62.1–72.9) and the overall 54.2% (44.1–64.0) (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: Two studies in Fig. 3, Floyd 2006 (36 of 51) and Zaytas 2013 (1500 of 2192, the largest study), have no entry in the reference list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The largest contributor to the lifetime pool (41% of its participants) cannot be identified from the article; Supplementary Table S1 (not read) may name it.

reporting_issues.issue: Risk-of-bias counts do not fit the groups: 2 of the 3 current-use studies are given as 50% and 15 of the 17 lifetime studies as 75% (3.4), while the low-risk re-analysis retains 14 lifetime studies (3.6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The low-risk results are reproduced with 14 studies (editors' calculation), so 14 of 17 is the likely count; the printed percentages are wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Values differ between Results and Discussion: CIPS in current use 55.2% (p. 4; Fig. 2) against 55.7% (p. 6); lifetime overall 55.6% (pp. 4, 6) against 54.7% (p. 6); PRISM 11.7% (p. 5) against 11.6% (p. 6). Labelling slips: the lifetime subgroup paragraph is introduced as being about the current-use group (p. 4); three PRISM (CIPD) studies are said to need extraction of CIPS prevalence (p. 4); Europe is labelled Spain and France (p. 5) although no included study is listed from France itself (p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the Results and figure values; the slips do not change the estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: One printed interval is not symmetric on the logit scale used for pooling: the all-dependent subgroup, 54.3% (44.8–67.2) (p. 5); every other interval in the text is (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: One bound is probably mistyped; do not cite this subgroup.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria list cross-sectional, case-control and cohort designs (p. 2), but three laboratory cocaine-challenge studies were included, two of which make up two thirds of the current-use group (p. 3; Fig. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: The current-use prevalence mixes paranoia induced in the laboratory with clinical diagnoses and should not be cited as a prevalence in people who currently use cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: Dates and sources: the search is dated to 31 August 2020 (p. 2) but the manuscript was received on 7 August 2020 (p. 1), and the flow chart lists two trial registries (p. 3) that the Methods do not mention.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a search update during revision, but undocumented; the search cannot be reproduced exactly from the article.
